title: AI Fundamentals (What is AI?)
overview: Understand the difference between rule-based and learning systems, what LLMs actually do, where they excel, where they fail, and when to keep a human in the loop.
coreContent:
1) Traditional Software vs Machine Learning

Rule-based software follows explicit logic written by developers (e.g., IF income > X THEN rate = Y). It is transparent and deterministic but brittle when conditions change. Machine Learning (ML) learns patterns from data. Instead of listing every feature of a cat, a model trained on many examples learns what makes a cat recognizable. ML adapts to new inputs but requires data curation and evaluation.

  • Good fit for rules: clear, stable policies; compliance checks; fixed pricing tiers.
  • Good fit for ML: fuzzy boundaries; many edge cases; natural language; vision; personalization.

2) What Large Language Models Actually Do

LLMs are sequence models that predict the next token given prior tokens. From this simple skill emerge powerful capabilities:

  • Summarise long text into executive briefs or bullets.
  • Classify emails, cases, or contacts by intent or priority.
  • Extract entities like names, amounts, dates, and policy references.
  • Draft emails, reports, proposals, or code.

Important: LLMs model language regularities, not verified facts. Un-grounded generations may be fluent yet wrong.

3) Typical Failure Modes

  • Hallucinations: confident statements that are not supported by sources.
  • Stale knowledge: training cut-offs miss recent changes.
  • Mis-specified tasks: vague instructions create outputs at the wrong level or for the wrong audience.
  • Missing inputs: requests to summarise or compare without attaching the materials.

4) Mitigations that Raise Reliability

  • Structured prompts & outputs: specify audience, tone, and format (JSON, table, bullets with limits).
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): inject passages from trusted sources; ask the model to cite them.
  • Tool use: offload math, lookups, and system actions to deterministic tools; the model orchestrates.
  • Human-in-the-Loop (HIL): require review for legal, financial, HR, or customer-impacting outputs; escalate on low confidence.

5) Human-in-the-Loop Triggers (practical)

  • High stakes decisions or irreversible actions.
  • Ambiguous instructions or missing data.
  • Unfamiliar edge cases or novel scenarios.
  • Model confidence signals are low or conflicting.

6) Mini-Checklist

  • Is the task clearly framed with a desired format?
  • Are the required documents or data attached?
  • Should retrieval be used to ground facts?
  • Who signs off if the output is used externally?

questions.question: LLMs are best described as systems that…
options: store verified facts like a database
predict the next token based on context
questions.answer: predict the next token based on context
questions.explanation: LLMs generate text by predicting the next token; they don’t guarantee factual accuracy without grounding.

questions.question: When should a Human-in-the-Loop be mandatory?
questions.explanation: Escalate when risk is high, instructions are ambiguous, or confidence is low.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
options: Injecting relevant evidence into the prompt
questions.answer: Injecting relevant evidence into the prompt
questions.explanation: RAG grounds outputs in authoritative sources, reducing hallucinations.

questions.question: Which is a common failure mode of LLMs?
questions.explanation: Fluent but incorrect outputs occur without proper grounding or guardrails.

questions.question: Which mitigation most directly improves reliability?
questions.explanation: Clear formats reduce ambiguity and make validation easier.

title: Landscape of Options (ChatGPT, Gemini, NotebookLM, Claude, Llama)
overview: Choose the right AI platform by comparing hosted services and open-weight models. Understand trade-offs in speed, control, security, and cost, and use examples to guide your decision.
coreContent:
1) Hosted Models: Speed, Scale, Simplicity

Hosted models are run by providers like OpenAI (ChatGPT), Google (Gemini, NotebookLM), and Anthropic (Claude). You access them via the cloud while the vendor manages servers, scaling, updates, and security patches in the background.

  • Pros: Quickest way to start; elastic scaling (handles surges automatically); built-in enterprise controls like SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and usage quotas.
  • Best when: You need results fast; vendor-managed infrastructure is preferred; strong SLAs and regular updates are important.
  • Trade-offs: Data residency may be limited; you depend on the vendor’s roadmap; costs grow with heavy usage (pay-as-you-go model).

Example: A marketing team uses ChatGPT to draft social media copy and Gemini inside Google Docs to polish proposals without managing servers or updates.

2) Open-Weight Models: Control & Customisation

Open-weight models (e.g., Meta’s Llama family) can be run in your own cloud (VPC) or on-premises. You get full control over how and where the model operates, but you also carry full responsibility for operations.

  • Pros: Keeps sensitive data local; allows fine-tuned safety guardrails; deeply integrates with internal systems and workflows.
  • Best when: Strict compliance or isolation is needed (e.g., financial services, healthcare, government) and your team has strong ML/MLOps capabilities.
  • Trade-offs: You must handle GPUs, scaling, monitoring, evaluations, and patching. This adds cost and complexity.

Example: A bank hosts Llama inside its secure data center to ensure customer information never leaves its network.

3) Fit-by-Scenario Guide

  • Gemini: Best for teams working heavily in Gmail, Docs, Sheets, and Slides.
  • ChatGPT: Strong for general-purpose drafting, rapid assistant building (Custom GPTs), and developer ecosystem support.
  • Claude: Suited for reviewing long documents, careful tone in communication, and producing business-friendly summaries.
  • Llama (open-weight): Chosen when self-hosting, strict policies, or isolation are non-negotiable.
  • NotebookLM: Ideal for research and Q&A over curated documents, providing citations and structured notebooks.

4) Risks & Mitigations

  • Vendor lock-in: Reduce risk by keeping prompts, data, and tools portable across platforms.
  • Residency/control: Validate where data is stored; select self-hosting for strict regions or regulated industries.
  • Safety posture: Guardrails differ between vendors; always run internal evaluations and keep humans in the loop for sensitive outputs.
  • Cost predictability: Set usage budgets and quotas; keep prompts concise; forecast based on actual consumption.

Example: A compliance team ensures all AI-generated legal drafts are reviewed by a lawyer before sending, while IT sets token quotas to avoid budget overruns.

5) Procurement & Governance Checklist

Before adopting a model, run through this checklist:

  • Security review: How does the vendor handle, retain, and store data? In which regions?
  • Admin controls: Ensure support for SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and usage quotas/budgets.
  • Compliance mapping: Check certifications and agreements (SOC2, ISO, GDPR/DPA terms, handling of PII/PHI).
  • Support model: Verify SLA coverage and support responsiveness.
  • Exit strategy: Confirm you can export or migrate prompts, data, and workflows to avoid lock-in.

questions.answer: Lower engineering overhead and faster time-to-value

questions.answer: Research grounded in your curated sources

title: LLMs Explained (How they differ)
overview: Understand how Large Language Models (LLMs) work, what drives quality, cost, and latency, and how retrieval, tools, and multimodality extend their capabilities.
coreContent:
1) Transformer Basics

Modern LLMs are based on the Transformer architecture. The key idea is self-attention, which allows the model to decide which words in a sequence are most important to each other. For example, in the sentence “The cat sat on the mat because it was tired”, the model needs to know that “it” refers to the cat, not the mat. By tracking these relationships across thousands of words, Transformers can preserve meaning over long passages.

During training, the model is exposed to billions of text samples and adjusts billions of parameters. The goal is simple: get better at predicting the next token. From this humble ability, powerful applications emerge ,summarisation, drafting, translation, reasoning, and more.

2) Tokens & Cost Drivers

LLMs don’t see whole words, they see tokens ,small units of text that may be subwords, full words, or punctuation marks.

  • Total tokens = prompt tokens + completion tokens. Both affect cost and speed.
  • Example: “Artificial Intelligence” may be 2 tokens, while “AI” is just 1.
  • Bigger models can be more accurate, but they are slower and more expensive per token.
  • External tool calls (like running a calculation or database query) add latency but return precise results instead of guesses.

Every extra sentence costs tokens. That’s why prompt engineering matters ,concise, relevant inputs keep costs down and responses sharp.

3) Decoding Controls

When generating text, models don’t always choose the single “most likely” word. They sample from probabilities, and you can adjust how that sampling works:

  • Temperature: Higher = more creative and varied answers (good for brainstorming). Lower = more predictable (good for compliance or legal writing).
  • Top-p (nucleus sampling): The model looks at the top set of most probable words (e.g., top 10%) and chooses from there. This balances variety with reliability.
  • Max tokens: Sets a hard cap on how long the output can be. Prevents runaway responses and controls costs.

Example: At high temperature, the model might invent a playful poem. At low temperature, it will stick to factual bullet points.

4) Context Windows & Salience

Models have a maximum context window ,the total number of tokens they can process at once. Newer models can handle hundreds of pages of text, but more isn’t always better. If you give irrelevant or repetitive text, the model can get distracted.

  • Put the most important content at the top of the prompt.
  • Remove filler and duplicated sections.
  • Use retrieval to pull in only the sections that matter.

Example: Instead of dumping a 200-page policy, retrieve just the 3 sections relevant to the employee’s question and feed those in.

5) Retrieval & Tooling

LLMs become far more powerful when combined with external systems:

  • Retrieval: Pull relevant information from a knowledge base or document library. This grounds the model’s answers and allows citations.
  • Tools: Offload specific tasks the model isn’t great at, like math, real-time data, or precise database lookups. Examples include calculators, CRM queries, or web searches.

Example: Instead of asking the LLM to “guess” a currency conversion, have it call a financial API and return the real-time value.

6) Multimodality

Newer LLMs aren’t just text-based ,they are multimodal, meaning they can take different input types like images, audio, or PDFs alongside text.

  • Example uses: Read a receipt image and extract line items, analyse a chart and describe trends, or answer questions about a PDF table.
  • When to use: Only when the non-text input adds real value. Otherwise, stick to text to save cost and reduce complexity.

title: Prompts 101
overview: Prompts are micro-specifications ,like writing a mini brief for the AI. Clear, structured prompts make outputs more reliable, business-ready, and easier to reuse.
coreContent:
1) ROO Structure (Role, Objective, Outcome)

A simple way to design prompts is the ROO framework:

  • Role: Tell the AI who it should act as. Example: “You are a procurement analyst.” This sets tone and expertise.
  • Objective: Define the task and focus. Example: “Compare vendors focusing on security and price.”
  • Outcome: Specify the format. Example: “Return a 6-row table with columns: Vendor, Strengths, Risks, Price.”

Analogy: Think of it like briefing a new team member. If you only say “do analysis,” you’ll get inconsistent work. But if you specify role, task, and output, you’ll get repeatable results.

2) CLEAR Framework

For more complex prompts, layer on CLEAR:

  • Context: Provide background or link relevant docs. Example: “Use the attached policy doc.”
  • Length: Limit the response size. Example: “No more than 200 words or 5 bullets.”
  • Explicitness: Define rules and edge cases. Example: “If a vendor has missing data, mark as ‘Unknown.’”
  • Audience: Tailor the response. Example: “Write for executives vs engineers.”
  • Response: Fix the format. Example: “Output in JSON or table.”

Tip: CLEAR prevents vague, open-ended answers by making every requirement explicit.

3) Templates You Can Reuse

Reusable prompt templates save time and improve consistency:

  • Summarise: “Summarise for audience in <120 words; include 3 risks.”
  • Classify: “Return JSON {intent, urgency, owner} using the rules below.”
  • Extract: “From the text, extract {name, date, amount}. If missing, return null.”

Example: Customer service teams can classify support tickets by intent (complaint, feature request, billing) using one standard prompt.

4) Clarify & Abstain Rules

AI should not guess when key inputs are missing:

  • If details are unclear, ask up to three clarifying questions.
  • If inputs are incomplete, respond with “Insufficient information provided” and list what’s needed.

Example: Instead of inventing numbers for a missing sales figure, the AI should ask: “Do you want me to proceed without Q2 data?”

5) Anti-Patterns

Avoid these common mistakes that lead to weak results:

  • Open-ended asks without specifying an audience or outcome. Example: “Write something about suppliers.”
  • Dumping long documents without any question or focus.
  • Changing output format every time (hard for automation).

Rule of thumb: Treat prompts like briefs for a contractor ,the clearer the instructions, the better the outcome.

title: Custom Assistants (Custom GPTs & Gems)
overview: Custom assistants combine rules, curated knowledge, and tools. They are like specialised co-workers: trained to follow house rules, consult trusted documents, and take approved actions. Publishing requires careful governance with versioning, testing, and role-based permissions.
coreContent:
1) Assistant Anatomy

A well-designed assistant has three main parts:

  • System prompt (rules): Sets the assistant’s personality, objectives, and guardrails. Example: “You are a customer support assistant. Always be polite, cite the policy document, and escalate if refund requests exceed $500.”
  • Knowledge: The library of curated documents it can draw on (manuals, policies, price lists). These documents ground answers in fact instead of guesses.
  • Tools: External actions the assistant is allowed to perform (e.g., calculator, CRM lookup, order tracking API). Tools extend capabilities beyond text generation.

2) System Prompt Skeleton

A reusable skeleton helps teams write consistent prompts:

Goal: 
Scope: 
Tone: 
Safety: 
Output format:

Example: For an HR assistant → Goal: answer leave policy questions; Scope: internal HR handbook only; Tone: friendly but professional; Safety: escalate legal queries; Output: concise bullet points.

3) Knowledge Hygiene

Assistants are only as good as their knowledge base. Poorly managed references lead to outdated or wrong answers.

  • Use only authoritative sources; remove outdated versions promptly.
  • Chunk long documents into smaller sections and add clear titles/metadata so retrieval is accurate.
  • Include worked examples (“If an invoice is overdue, respond with template A”) to guide the model.

Example: A sales assistant should reference only the current year’s price list, not archived versions.

4) Tooling Guidelines

Tools must be carefully defined and monitored to prevent misuse:

  • Clearly document each tool’s purpose, inputs, and outputs.
  • Apply guardrails ,e.g., require approval for sensitive write actions (like updating a customer record).
  • Log every call for auditing; include budgets and timeouts to avoid runaway costs.
  • Return structured errors so failures don’t confuse users.

Example: A finance assistant may use a calculator tool for percentages, but cannot approve payments without human review.

5) Publishing & Governance

Moving an assistant from idea to production is a structured process:

  • Versioning: Track every change to prompts and configs; keep a CHANGELOG with quality notes.
  • Testing: Use evaluation sets at each stage (staging → pilot → production) to measure accuracy and safety.
  • RBAC: Restrict who can edit rules, upload knowledge, or enable tools. Not everyone should have production access.

Example: A legal assistant is tested with 50 past case queries before rollout. Only the legal ops team can edit its scope or upload new references.

questions.explanation: Curated, current sources form the foundation for reliable answers.

title: Agentic AI (What & Why)
overview: Unlike simple chatbots, agents can perceive, plan, act, and adjust using tools. This makes them powerful but also riskier ,so they must be built with strong controls, observability, and human oversight.
coreContent:
1) Agent vs Chatbot

A chatbot responds turn-by-turn: you ask, it answers. An agent goes further ,it breaks down tasks, decides on steps, uses tools, checks results, and loops until the goal is achieved.

Example: A chatbot might answer, “Your order is in progress.” An agent could check the order system, see the delivery date, email the courier API if delayed, and return a detailed update.

2) Perception → Plan → Act Loop

Agents follow a feedback loop that mirrors human problem-solving:

  • Perception: Understand the request and gather relevant context (e.g., fetch customer profile).
  • Plan: Break into steps, choose the right tools, and order the actions logically.
  • Act: Execute tool calls, evaluate outcomes, and adjust if needed ,repeating until the goal is achieved.

Example: An IT support agent perceives “reset password,” plans steps (check identity → reset in Active Directory → confirm by email), and acts using APIs and workflows until complete.

3) Control Plane

Without boundaries, agents could loop endlessly or take unsafe actions. Controls keep them safe and predictable:

  • Budgets: Cap token spend, runtime, or number of tool calls per run.
  • Whitelists: Restrict access to approved tools, APIs, or domains only.
  • Approval gates: Require human sign-off before sensitive actions (e.g., issuing refunds or updating payroll).

Analogy: Think of an intern with a corporate credit card. You’d set spending limits and approvals ,the same applies to AI agents.

4) Observability

You can’t govern what you can’t see. Observability ensures you know what the agent is doing:

  • Structured logs: Record every decision, input, and tool call.
  • Traces: Follow an end-to-end workflow across multiple steps.
  • Metrics: Track success rate, cost per run, actions per run, and escalation frequency.

Example: A customer support agent’s logs reveal it escalates 20% of refund requests ,signalling either policy gaps or over-escalation.

5) Safety Rubric

Agents can be powerful, so safety rules are critical:

  • No irreversible actions (e.g., deleting accounts, sending payments) without explicit approval.
  • Always log inputs/outputs, and redact sensitive data (passwords, card numbers).
  • Fail safe: if uncertain or low-confidence, escalate to a human instead of guessing.

Example: A finance agent can draft an invoice but cannot send it without human review, ensuring accountability.

title: Agentic Workflows (n8n & Python)
overview: Agentic workflows combine LLM reasoning with orchestration and custom logic. Use n8n to schedule, route, and integrate systems; use Python for validation, calculations, and testing. Design with reliability, observability, and security in mind.
coreContent:
1) Separation of Concerns

Think of agentic workflows as a team with different roles:

  • Reasoning (LLM): Handles planning, drafting, and interpreting inputs. Example: “Summarise the customer email and decide next steps.”
  • Orchestration (n8n): Manages sequencing, retries, and integrations. Example: Route the AI’s decision to Slack, Salesforce, and email.
  • Custom logic (Python): Adds exact rules, validations, or calculations. Example: Recalculate VAT correctly before sending an invoice.

Analogy: The LLM is the strategist, n8n is the project manager, and Python is the specialist engineer.

2) n8n Building Blocks

n8n is a low-code workflow platform that connects systems together:

  • Triggers: Events that start a workflow, like “email received,” “webhook hit,” or “run every Monday 9am.”
  • Nodes: Steps in the flow, such as transforming data, calling an API, or writing to a database/Google Sheet.
  • Credentials vault: A secure place to store API keys and tokens. Never hardcode secrets into workflows.

Example: A support ticket workflow triggers when a new Zendesk ticket arrives, calls an LLM to classify urgency, and routes high-priority cases to PagerDuty.

3) Python Add-ons

Sometimes low-code isn’t enough. Use Python for:

  • Pre/post-processing: Clean raw text before feeding it to the model; validate that outputs are valid JSON.
  • Complex algorithms: Perform calculations (e.g., discount formulas, risk scoring) the LLM shouldn’t guess.
  • Unit tests: Lock in behaviour and detect regressions when prompts or workflows change.

Example: In a finance workflow, Python ensures rounding rules are always applied consistently before updating the ledger.

4) Reliability Recipes

Workflows need resilience ,failures should degrade gracefully, not cause chaos:

  • Exponential backoff: Retry transient failures like timeouts, adding longer delays between attempts.
  • Idempotency keys: Prevent duplicate charges or entries if a step is retried. (E.g., ensure a payment is only processed once.)
  • Observability: Use structured logs with correlation IDs so each request can be traced end-to-end.

Example: If an API call fails due to rate limits, the workflow retries after 1s, then 2s, then 4s, instead of hammering the service.

5) Secret Management

Workflows often connect to sensitive systems. Treat secrets carefully:

  • Use a vault or Key Management System (KMS).
  • Rotate API keys regularly.
  • Grant the minimum permissions required (“least privilege”).
  • Never print or log secrets ,redact them in observability tools.

Example: A workflow using Google APIs stores OAuth tokens in n8n’s vault and rotates them automatically, ensuring no developer ever sees the raw secret.

questions.question: An orchestrator (e.g., n8n) primarily…
questions.explanation: It coordinates tasks; the model handles reasoning.

questions.question: Retries with exponential backoff address…
questions.explanation: Increasing delay avoids overloading services and respects limits.

questions.question: Secrets should be…
questions.explanation: Use a vault/KMS, rotate keys, and avoid logging them.

questions.question: Idempotency protects against…
questions.explanation: Ensures retries don’t double-charge or duplicate records.

options: Custom logic and tests are needed
questions.answer: Custom logic and tests are needed
questions.explanation: Complex workflows or precision logic often require code.

title: Use-Case Identification
overview: Identify high-value, feasible AI opportunities by linking everyday pain points to proven AI patterns. Use baselines and readiness checks to focus efforts where ROI is measurable and adoption is realistic.
coreContent:
1) Spotting Inefficiencies

Good AI use-cases often solve problems that frustrate employees or customers. Look for inefficiencies such as:

  • Repetition: Tasks people copy/paste daily (e.g., updating the same status reports).
  • Volume: Many small tasks that add up (e.g., processing hundreds of customer emails).
  • Delay: Work stuck in queues or requiring summaries (e.g., waiting for analysts to condense meeting notes).
  • Error-prone: Manual re-keying or inconsistent formatting (e.g., sales data entered differently by each rep).

Example: A support team spends 20 minutes per ticket classifying and routing issues ,high repetition and high volume make this a great AI candidate.

2) Map to AI Patterns

Most business pain points map to a handful of repeatable AI patterns:

  • Summarise: Turn meeting transcripts into concise notes.
  • Classify: Route tickets by urgency or department.
  • Extract: Pull invoice numbers or dates from messy text.
  • Generate: Draft emails, FAQs, or reports.
  • Translate: Convert technical docs into plain language or across languages.
  • Plan/Reason: Suggest project steps or compare options.

Tip: If a pain point fits one of these patterns, it’s usually feasible with current AI.

3) Discovery Questions

Use structured questions to uncover opportunities:

  • Where do people copy/paste the same info repeatedly?
  • Which tasks pile up in backlogs or long wait times?
  • What requires reading many pages to extract key facts?
  • Which errors or rework create the most friction or cost?

Example: In HR, employees often ask the same five leave-policy questions ,repetitive, low-risk, and easy to automate.

4) Baselines Before Build

Before piloting AI, capture a baseline to prove ROI:

  • Minutes spent per task.
  • Frequency of the task per day/week/month.
  • Number of users performing the task.
  • Error/rework rate and cost of corrections.

Example: If analysts spend 30 hours/month summarising reports, you can compare post-AI usage to show time saved and justify scaling.

5) Readiness Signals

Even if the opportunity looks good, check for readiness:

  • Clear owner and champion: Someone accountable for adoption.
  • Data access: Availability of sample documents or records.
  • Risk profile: Low–medium risk and measurable value is best for early wins.

Example: A finance department with clean invoice data and a motivated sponsor is far more ready than an unowned process with sensitive data and no champion.

questions.question: Great candidates for AI are typically…
questions.explanation: Automation returns the most value where volume and repetition exist.

questions.question: Creating meeting notes usually combines which patterns?
questions.explanation: Condense the discussion and produce a structured draft.

questions.question: Why capture baseline time before a pilot?
questions.explanation: Without a baseline, improvements are not defensible.

questions.question: A red flag for a ‘good’ use-case is…
questions.explanation: Risk without controls undermines adoption.

questions.question: Stakeholders are…
questions.explanation: Involve owners, sponsors, and end users early.

title: Prioritisation & ROI
overview: Learn how to prioritise AI opportunities using value, effort, and risk. Calculate financial impact with formulas for monthly value, ROI, and payback period, and use sensitivity analysis to test assumptions.
coreContent:
1) Prioritisation Dimensions

Not every AI idea is equal. Use three dimensions to compare opportunities:

  • Value: How much time, cost, or risk it saves (e.g., fewer manual hours, reduced rework, lower compliance exposure).
  • Effort: Complexity of data access, integration requirements, and engineering lift.
  • Risk: Compliance concerns, customer impact, or change management challenges.

Example: Automating meeting notes may be high value/low effort, while automating legal contract review may be high value but high risk.

2) Monthly Value Formula

Quantify benefits in monetary terms using this baseline formula:

Monthly Value = (Time Saved per Task × Frequency × Users × Hourly Rate) + Error-Cost Reduction

Example: If 5 analysts each save 15 minutes per day, the total value is (15/60 × $40 × 22 days × 5 users) = $1,100/month, plus any measurable error-cost reductions.

3) ROI & Payback

Return on Investment (ROI) helps justify spend to executives. Use this 12-month formula:

12-Month ROI = ((12 × Value) − Build Cost − (12 × Run Cost)) / (Build Cost + (12 × Run Cost)) × 100

The payback period is the month when cumulative benefits equal cumulative costs.

Rule of thumb: Projects with payback <12 months are highly attractive for early adoption.

4) Worked Example

10 users × 20 minutes saved per day × 22 workdays × $35/hr ≈ $2,567/month.

Build cost = $12k; Run cost = $400/month. At full adoption, payback ≈ 5.3 months.

Interpretation: Even if adoption is only 60%, the payback is under 9 months, making this a solid case.

5) Sensitivity Analysis

Assumptions rarely hold perfectly. Test scenarios by varying key drivers:

  • Adoption: What if only 30% of users adopt? 60%? 90%?
  • Time saved: Is it consistently 15 minutes, or could it be 10–20?
  • Error-cost reduction: Count only when documented with evidence.

Example: Sensitivity analysis shows that even with 50% adoption, the project breaks even in year one ,building confidence in the investment.

6) Prioritisation Matrix (Risk × Reward)

Visualise projects on a two-by-two grid:

  • High Reward / Low Risk: Start here ,they are quick wins.
  • High Reward / High Risk: Worth exploring later with guardrails.
  • Low Reward / Low Risk: Low impact, but easy to try.
  • Low Reward / High Risk: Usually not worth pursuing.

title: Pilot to Production
overview: Many AI initiatives die in ‘POC purgatory.’ To avoid stall, move in phases with clear exit criteria, service-level objectives (SLOs), observability, and robust fallbacks. Each stage should earn trust before scaling.
coreContent:
1) Phased Progression

Progress in deliberate steps to build confidence and avoid wasted investment:

  • POC (Proof of Concept): Validate feasibility using sample or synthetic data. Goal = “Does it work at all?”
  • Pilot: Deploy to a small group inside real workflows. Capture metrics (accuracy, time saved) and qualitative feedback (user trust).
  • Limited Production: Expand to more users with operational runbooks, monitoring, and support processes in place.
  • Scale: Roll out broadly across the org with mature governance, training, and performance reviews.

Example: An HR chatbot first answers 100 sample leave-policy queries (POC), then supports one department (Pilot), then expands company-wide (Scale).

2) Exit Criteria (per stage)

Each stage must have clear success criteria before moving forward:

  • Target quality: Evaluation set results meet threshold (e.g., ≥90% precision/recall).
  • Cost & latency: Each run stays within defined budget (e.g., <$0.05 per request; <2s response).
  • Safety checks: Escalation works; model abstains or flags low-confidence cases.

Tip: “Done” must be measurable, not subjective. No exit criteria = stall.

3) SLOs & Observability

Service-Level Objectives (SLOs) make quality expectations explicit and trackable:

  • Accuracy (e.g., ≥85% agreement with human evaluators).
  • Latency (e.g., <3s response for 95% of queries).
  • Cost (e.g., <$1 per 1,000 queries).

Use logs, traces, and dashboards to spot drift, failures, or regressions. Alerts should trigger when thresholds are breached.

Example: A dashboard shows rising latency after a new prompt version → rollback before user complaints grow.

4) Fallbacks & Rollback

AI should degrade gracefully instead of failing silently:

  • Fallbacks: Human review, simpler model, or rule-based system. Example: If invoice extraction fails, send the file to an analyst.
  • Rollback: Version everything (prompts, configs, code). Keep a “rollback button” with a pre-flight checklist to revert safely.

Rule: Never deploy a model you can’t instantly roll back.

5) Common Stall Points

Most projects stall for predictable reasons. Watch out for:

  • No owner or champion; unclear approvals.
  • No evaluation data to measure progress.
  • Data access delays blocking pilots.
  • Poor change management or lack of training for end users.

Example: A legal AI pilot stalls because there’s no agreed quality metric ,lawyers disagree if it’s “good enough.” Define criteria early.

title: Everyday Integration (Workspace)
overview: AI delivers the most impact when embedded directly into daily tools like Gmail, Docs, Sheets, and Slides. This module explores practical integrations and the guardrails needed to balance productivity with governance.
coreContent:
1) Gmail

Email is often the biggest productivity drain. AI can help by:

  • Summarising threads: Condense 30-message chains into a 5-bullet recap with action items (task, owner, due date).
  • Drafting replies: Suggest concise, context-aware responses with proposed next steps.
  • Routing/classification: Automatically tag, label, or assign ownership (e.g., sales vs support).

Example: Instead of reading a long thread about a customer issue, AI provides a one-paragraph summary plus a draft response for approval.

2) Docs

Docs are where narratives live. AI adds value through:

  • Outlines & first drafts: Turn a 3-bullet idea into a structured outline or rough draft.
  • Summaries: Condense 10-page reports into a 1-page executive brief.
  • Evaluator prompts: Check writing for clarity, tone, bias, or completeness before sharing externally.

Example: A policy draft can be automatically checked for jargon, bias, and missing sections.

3) Sheets

AI transforms Sheets into more than rows and columns:

  • Classification: Tag rows by urgency, sentiment, or category.
  • Light analytics: Suggest pivots, identify trends, or highlight anomalies.
  • Structuring data: Convert messy notes into clean, structured tables.

Example: A sales ops analyst pastes 200 call notes, and AI extracts {client, date, outcome} into a structured table.

4) Slides

Slide decks are storytelling tools. AI accelerates creation by:

  • Docs → Slides conversion: Turn a written outline into a draft deck with slides and speaker notes.
  • Story flow suggestions: Recommend logical order of sections or polish bullet text.

Example: An annual report draft in Docs can generate a starter slide deck in minutes.

5) Governance Guardrails

Embedding AI in everyday tools increases risk if guardrails are missing. Always enforce:

  • Data policy: Never input unapproved personally identifiable information (PII).
  • Fact-checking: Verify all critical outputs before external or executive use.
  • Auditability: Keep logs of prompts and outputs; restrict advanced features by role.

Example: A finance analyst using AI to summarise budgets must still verify numbers before sharing with executives.
